t: Prime Arrangements — Counting Permutations with Primes on Prime Indices
o: We need permutations of 1..n where every prime *value* sits at a prime *index*. The key observation: the condition only couples primes with primes and composites (plus 1) with non-prime indices. So if there are $p$ primes among 1..n, the $p$ prime values can be arranged freely among the $p$ prime indices ($p!$ ways), and the remaining $n-p$ values arrange freely among the $n-p$ other indices ($(n-p)!$ ways). Answer: $p! \cdot (n-p)! \bmod 10^9+7$. For n=5, primes are {2,3,5} so p=3, answer = 3!·2! = 12. For n=100, p=25, giving 25!·75! mod 1e9+7 = 682289015. With n ≤ 100, any reasonable method works; we just need to count primes correctly.
k: Only the count of primes p matters — the answer is p! · (n−p)! mod 10^9+7.
Count primes up to 100 with trial division or a sieve; both are trivially fast at this scale.
Compute factorials iteratively modulo 10^9+7 to avoid overflow.

a.n: Approach 1: Trial Division Prime Count + Factorials
a.i: For each number from 2 to n, test primality by checking divisors up to its square root. Count primes p, then multiply p! by (n−p)! under the modulus. This is the most direct translation of the math insight into code.
s: Define isPrime(x): check divisibility by integers 2..sqrt(x).
Count p = number of primes in [2, n].
Compute f1 = p! mod M and f2 = (n−p)! mod M iteratively.
a.t: O(n·√n) — for each of n numbers we trial-divide up to √x; trivial for n ≤ 100.

a.i: Since n ≤ 100, a Sieve of Eratosthenes counts all primes in one pass, replacing per-number trial division. This is the canonical 'prime number sieve' approach and scales gracefully if constraints were much larger.
s: Build a boolean array isComposite of size n+1.
For each i from 2 to √n, mark multiples i², i²+i, ... as composite.
Count p = number of unmarked entries ≥ 2.
a.t: O(n log log n) — standard Sieve of Eratosthenes complexity, plus O(n) factorial computation.

w: In an interview, state the counting argument first (primes go to prime indices independently of everything else), then pick either approach — the sieve signals stronger fundamentals, but trial division is perfectly fine at n ≤ 100. Pitfalls: forgetting that index 1 is not prime even though value 1 must be handled (it belongs to the non-prime group); computing full factorials before taking the modulus (overflow in C++/Java); mishandling n=1 (answer is 1, since 1!·0!). Edge cases: n=1 → 1, n=2 → 1 (both prime, 2!=... wait, 2!·0! = 2? No — check: primes are {2}, p=1, so 1!·1! = 1). A likely follow-up: what if n were up to 10^7? Then precompute factorials once or use a linear sieve, but the formula stays identical.
